title: The Space Between: Artist Statement
body:
There are no people in these photographs. That is deliberate.

We live inside a constant stream of information. Our attention has become a commodity, harvested and sold, and stillness has grown rare enough to feel almost radical. In that climate, wanting to be alone can look like a retreat. I see it differently. Solitude is not the absence of connection; it is the condition that makes real attention possible. The photographs in The Space Between are about that condition: silence, stillness, grounding, and the peace that arrives when the noise finally falls away.

In the seventeenth century, Blaise Pascal observed that most of humanity’s troubles come from our inability to sit quietly, alone, in a room. Two centuries later, Henry David Thoreau went to the woods because he wished to live deliberately. Neither was running from the world. Both were looking for a clearer way to stand in it. Today that search feels more urgent, and harder, than ever.

The title refers to the spaces between things. Japanese aesthetics has a word for this, ma: the interval in space and time, the pause, the silence between things that does not need to be filled. Matsumoto Kiyoshi writes that without ma, “the world would be a continuous blur of action and matter without meaning.” Ma is what gives a moment its edges, so that words, sounds and actions take on clarity. It is the rest in a piece of music that gives meaning to the note before it and the note that follows, the respite between activity, the pause between thoughts.

間

ma
門 gate + 日 sun

The character for ma joins two others: 門, a gate, and 日, the sun. Matsumoto calls it “the gateway of illumination of all things.” I know of no better description of a photograph. The gate is the frame: the edges of the camera’s view, the boundaries of a composition. The sun is light, the one material every photograph is made of. A photograph is light admitted through a gate, and what the frame holds is not the whole world but an interval of it, set apart so that it can be seen and appreciated.

My photographs work the same way. Their subject is not the absence of things but the relationship between them: the interval between two trees, between a ridgeline and the sky, between light arriving and light leaving. That space lets each element breathe and connect, with one another and with you. Space, light, and quiet are not what is left over in these photographs. They are the subject and the invitation.

Throughout my career, I have worked in the panoramic format. The wide slice mirrors the way we take in a landscape, and it puts the viewer in a position to enter the picture, or to feel that they are already standing in it. The format has deep roots in Japanese art: handscrolls and folding screens, such as Hasegawa Tōhaku’s Pine Trees, stretch the landscape into long forms that the eye travels slowly, where the mist and the intervals between the pines, ma made visible, carry as much meaning as the trees themselves. When one of these photographs works, it carries you to the moment something stopped me and asks you to step into the scene, not as a spectator of someone else’s experience, but as the one standing there. I am never lonely in these moments, and I hope you won’t be either.

The landscape has a long history as a place for contemplation, from Caspar David Friedrich, whose lone figures seen from behind stand in for the viewer, to the still water and glowing air of the American Luminists. In photography, Carleton Watkins’s mammoth-plate views of Yosemite carry that same hushed atmosphere: luminous light, deep stillness, granite walls mirrored in calm water. His pictures are credited with helping persuade Congress to protect the valley in 1864, early proof that an image of beauty can change how a society acts. My work belongs to this lineage.

Beauty has had an uneasy place in contemporary art. Serious work is often expected to expose, argue, or provoke, and photography has rightly earned its power to reveal injustice and shift public opinion. The New Topographics photographers, and those who followed them, such as Richard Misrach and Mark Klett, showed with real force what we have done to the land. I admire that work. But I also take to heart the argument the photographer Robert Adams made in Beauty in Photography: that beauty, rightly understood, is not a retreat from the world but a way of affirming it. The philosopher Elaine Scarry goes further, suggesting that beauty pulls us outside ourselves and toward care for something beyond us. A culture that can no longer pause to appreciate beauty has lost more than a pleasure. It has lost patience, humility, and the common ground of a world we all share.

I make images that leave room for reflection. They are a reminder to put down the screen, step outside, and remember that we belong to something larger and older than the arguments of the moment. Elevating subtle beauty is not naïve. In an age that rewards the loudest or most divisive voices, it may be one of the more hopeful things an artist can do.

I made these images for the joy of being there, not for an audience. The Space Between is the first time I have gathered them with you in mind. After thirty years of teaching photography, I believe the most important thing I can teach is how to notice. It is often said that beauty is in the eye of the beholder; I would argue that it is there for anyone who chooses to see it. My hope is that these photographs help you remember, or discover, a life free from the noise. A quiet space. The space between.
